lessons.title: Why analytics needs its own model
lessons.why: "Let's have the report just read the same database as the app" — a proposal that comes up on every other project. It saves a day at the start and costs months later. Being able to explain why this isn't done comes up before you even start building the model itself.
lessons.form:
A source (OLTP) answers "what's happening with this order right now" and is optimized for writes: data is spread across dozens of narrow tables, so one change touches one row.

A reporting model (OLAP) answers "what happened across all orders over two years" and is optimized for reads: wide fact tables with small lookup tables next to them.
lessons.example:
The requester's question: "revenue by category for the quarter."

In a reporting model that's one fact table and one product lookup: sum revenue, break it down by category. Two objects, one relationship.
lessons.reads: The report reads exactly the data it needs, without getting in the way of checkout — the model refreshes at night and lives apart from the production database.
lessons.wrong: The same question, as a query straight against the production database: join orders, order_lines, products, product_categories, category_tree, and sum by the top level of the tree.
lessons.wrongWhy: It will work — right up to the day fifty people open the report at once and a heavy query collides with the same database that's handling checkout. A second bill arrives later: the source's structure changes for the app's needs, not the report's, and one day a renamed column silently breaks the reporting.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask yourself: does this query compete for resources with whatever is making money right now? If yes, there needs to be a layer between it and the source.

lessons.title: Fact grain
lessons.why: The first question for any fact table is "what does one row mean." Without an answer, you can't sum correctly or compare honestly: two tables at different levels of detail in one report give numbers that are each correct on their own and meaningless side by side.
lessons.form:
Grain is written as a list joined by a multiplication sign — one dimension per factor:

  week × outlet × SKU

If that combination occurs exactly once in the table, the grain has been named correctly.
lessons.example: fact_sellout: one row is the sales of one SKU at one outlet for one week. There are 118,449 rows, and exactly that many distinct "week × outlet × SKU" combinations.
lessons.reads: The match between row count and combination count is the proof: the key isn't duplicated, so the grain is described exactly, not approximately.
lessons.wrong: "One row of fact_sellout is one purchase."
lessons.wrongWhy: The phrasing sounds natural and is almost always wrong: a register rings up dozens of receipts a week, while the table has one row per SKU for that week. It's already an aggregate, not an event. The mistake surfaces on "how many purchases were there" — this table has no answer to that at all, and people usually bring the row count instead of an answer.
lessons.selfCheck: Check it by counting: the row count and the count of distinct combinations of the key dimensions should match. If they don't, the grain is actually finer than you thought.

lessons.title: Star and snowflake
lessons.why: An extract arrives as one wide table, with product name, brand, category, city and region sitting right next to sales. The temptation to leave it as is is real — it works, doesn't it. The star schema is why it gets split into a fact table and lookups anyway.
lessons.form:
A fact is what gets measured and accumulated: units, revenue. A dimension is what you slice it by: product, outlet, date, promo.

  fact in the center, dimensions around it — a star
  a dimension split further — a snowflake
lessons.example: fact_sellout (118,449 rows) plus dim_product (47), dim_customer (144), dim_promo (89), dim_date. The "category" attribute sits as a column inside dim_product — five categories across forty-seven products.
lessons.reads: The product name is stored 47 times — once per product — not 118,449 times, once per sales row. Editing the name happens in one place and shows up in every report immediately.
lessons.wrong: Keep one flat table of 118,449 rows, where product_name, brand, category, city and region_name sit as columns next to revenue.
lessons.wrongWhy: The most expensive thing here isn't disk space — it's consistency. Rename a product and the edit has to be carried into every row it appeared in, and any row you miss turns into a stray extra category in the filter. And the reverse case: a product that never sold this year simply doesn't exist in a table like this, so a "sales by all SKUs" report has no row for it with a zero.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask of every column in the fact table: is it measured, or does it describe? If it describes, it belongs in a lookup table, where it's stored once.

lessons.title: Relationships and cardinality
lessons.why: A relationship in a model isn't the same thing as a JOIN in a query. A JOIN combines rows; a relationship sets the direction a filter will travel along it. A report where a slicer doesn't affect half the measures is almost always explained by exactly this.
lessons.form:
A relationship has two properties, and they must not be confused:

  cardinality — how many rows on each side correspond to one row on the other (one-to-many, many-to-many)
  filter direction — lookup to fact by default, not the reverse
lessons.example: dim_product (47 rows, product_id unique) → fact_sellout (118,449 rows): one-to-many. Pick brand «Nettora» in a slicer — the filter travels from lookup to fact, and the revenue sum computes across that brand's five products.
lessons.reads: The "one" side filters the "many" side: the lookup sets which fact rows take part in the calculation.
lessons.wrong: Expecting a slicer on promo in dim_promo to filter dim_product the same way — "show the products that took part in the promo."
lessons.wrongWhy: The filter will reach from dim_promo into fact_sellout, and stop there: it doesn't flow back into dim_product by default — that's the "many"-to-"one" direction. The product list stays at its full 47, and that isn't a bug, it's the default behaviour — turning the reverse direction on takes a deliberate choice, and it has a cost.
lessons.selfCheck: Before you get surprised by a number, trace the filter's path with your finger from the slicer to the table where the measure computes. Did it get there, and did it change direction along the way?

lessons.title: Two paths to the same table
lessons.why: The most expensive modeling mistake looks harmless: another relationship got added because "it's more convenient to filter this way." After that, the report either refuses to compute, or — worse — computes and returns a number several times bigger than the real one.
lessons.form: There should be exactly one path from a fact table to a lookup. If there are two, the model doesn't pick the better one — it either bans the second relationship (leaves it inactive), or, if the join is made directly in a query, multiplies rows across every match.
lessons.example: fact_sellout links to dim_promo by promo_id — that's the correct path: a sales row either has a promo or it doesn't. The table's total revenue is ¥126,911,191, and along this path it stays that way.
lessons.reads: One path, one value. Every sales row corresponds to exactly one promo, or none.
lessons.wrong: Add a second path: fact_sellout → dim_product by product_id, then dim_product → dim_promo by brand, because "a promo is set up per brand anyway."
lessons.wrongWhy: Each of the nine brands has 9 to 11 entries in the promo lookup, so every sales row matches all of its brand's promos at once. Row count becomes 1,173,847 instead of 118,449, and revenue becomes ¥1,262,668,596 instead of ¥126,911,191 — exactly tenfold. No single row is "wrong" in this: the join did precisely what it was asked to do.
lessons.selfCheck: Count the paths from a fact table to a lookup. More than one — either delete the extra one, or leave it inactive and switch it on explicitly inside a measure.

lessons.title: Measure or calculated column
lessons.why: Both approaches produce what looks like the same number in the field list, and confusing the two is the source of the single most common complaint: "the report shows the wrong thing once I add a slicer." It isn't a calculation mistake — a column and a measure answer different questions.
lessons.form:
A calculated column computes once at data refresh, is stored physically per row, and afterward behaves like ordinary data — a filter doesn't recompute it.

A measure doesn't store a value at all: it recomputes every time it's displayed, accounting for whatever filters are in effect at that moment.
lessons.example: Brand «Nettora»'s share of revenue is 12.7% across the whole database. Set up as a measure, it's DIVIDE(Nettora revenue, total revenue). Add a region slicer for «Tokyo» to the report — the measure recomputes and shows 19.1%, because both parts of the formula recomputed along with the slicer.
lessons.reads: A measure doesn't store the number "12.7%" anywhere — it stores a formula and evaluates it under whatever filter is in effect right now.
lessons.wrong: Set up the same share as a calculated column: compute it once across the whole database and put 12.7% into every fact row.
lessons.wrongWhy: After a Tokyo slicer, the column doesn't recompute — it holds the number that was written into it, not a formula, and it keeps showing 12.7% where the report expects 19.1%. Nothing about this looks wrong from the outside: there's a number, it looks plausible, and without checking against an independent calculation, a swap like this can go unnoticed for months.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask of every number in the model: does it have to change with a slicer, or not? Changes — a measure. Never changes (a product's category, say) — a column or a lookup attribute.

lessons.title: Filter context
lessons.why: The same measure shows different numbers in different cells of a report, and it isn't different formulas — it's different conditions the formula computes under. Being able to list those conditions for a specific cell is a basic skill for reading any report, not just your own.
lessons.form:
A cell's filter context is made up of everything acting on it at once:

  the matrix row, the matrix column,
  slicers on the page,
  filters built into the measure itself
lessons.example: A cell at the intersection of row «Tokyo» and a «Nettora» slicer: filter context is region = «Tokyo» AND brand = «Nettora». Revenue in that cell is ¥819,771. Remove the brand slicer — the context narrows to one condition, region = «Tokyo», and the same measure shows ¥3,718,723, the total across every brand.
lessons.reads: A cell doesn't "hold" a number — it sets the conditions a measure computes it under. Different cells in the same table almost always live in different filter contexts.
lessons.wrong: Assume that since it's the same measure (Revenue), the number must be the same in every cell of the report.
lessons.wrongWhy: A measure is a formula, not a result. The same formula, evaluated in different filter contexts, legitimately and expectedly gives different numbers: that isn't a bug, it's the whole reason measures exist — they don't need a separate formula for every slicer.
lessons.selfCheck: Before reading a number out of a cell, say out loud every condition acting on it: from the row, from the column, from the page's slicers. Miss one, and you won't understand where the number came from.

lessons.title: Row context
lessons.why: A calculated column meant to return one specific row's revenue instead shows the same huge number in every row at once. The cause is confusing two kinds of context, and without understanding that, the mistake looks inexplicable.
lessons.form:
A calculated column has row context: it "sees" the current row's values and can reference them directly.

But an aggregating function like SUM inside that column ignores row context — it only responds to filter context, and at the moment the column computes, there is none at all.
lessons.example: fact_sellout's first row: revenue = ¥398.31. A column "=SUM(fact_sellout[revenue])" in that same row shows not 398.31, but 126,911,191 — the sum of revenue across the whole table, because SUM is bounded by nothing except a filter, and there is none.
lessons.reads: A plain reference to the current row's column, with no aggregating function, is what genuinely uses row context: "=fact_sellout[revenue]" returns exactly 398.31.
lessons.wrong: Write a column "RowRevenue = SUM(fact_sellout[revenue])", expecting to get that row's own value.
lessons.wrongWhy: SUM is an aggregating function, built to add up a set of rows, not read one. Without an explicit transition from row context to filter context (that's what CALCULATE does), SUM sees an empty row context and aggregates whatever isn't filtered — meaning the entire table.
lessons.selfCheck: Does the calculated column's formula have an aggregating function (SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT)? If so, and you haven't wrapped it in CALCULATE — the result almost certainly isn't what you expected.

lessons.title: Measure additivity
lessons.why: Not every measure can be summed across every breakdown and give a meaningful number. The confusion here isn't about DAX syntax — it's about arithmetic: summing stock on hand the same way as revenue gives you a number that describes nothing.
lessons.form:
An additive measure sums across any dimension without losing meaning — revenue, units.

A semi-additive one sums across some dimensions and not across time — stock on hand.

A non-additive one doesn't sum at all — price, share, an average.
lessons.example: One distributor's stock for one SKU: October 768, November 1,055, December 1,315 — climbing, a sign of stockpiling ahead of a bonus. Summing these three months into a "quarterly stock total" is meaningless: you get 3,138, a number that never once existed in the warehouse at any moment in time.
lessons.reads: Stock sums perfectly normally across products and distributors within the same month — that's a horizontal slice. Summing it across months, along time, doesn't work: months aren't independent portions, they're snapshots of the same inventory.
lessons.wrong: Show "stock on hand for the year" on a report as SUM(units_on_hand) across all twelve months of 2025.
lessons.wrongWhy: The annual sum gives 370,142 — while actual stock at end of December was 52,350. A number sevenfold off the truth was arrived at with perfectly honest arithmetic — the question was simply put to the wrong function: annual stock is a value at a specific moment (usually period end), not a sum of monthly snapshots.
lessons.selfCheck: Before writing SUM, ask: does this quantity accumulate over a period (like revenue), or exist at every moment in time (like stock, price)? The second kind can't be summed across time.

lessons.title: The date table
lessons.why: The model already has dates — right there in the fact tables. It seems like a separate calendar shouldn't be needed: filter on those columns and you're done. The trap is that the date in one fact table and the date in another aren't the same column, and without a shared calendar there's no way to bring them under one slicer.
lessons.form:
A date table is a by-day lookup, with derived columns (week, month, quarter, year), connected to every fact table at once.

One slicer on this table filters every fact table simultaneously, even when they have different native time granularity.
lessons.example: dim_date's row for March 3rd 2025: date_id = week_start = 2025-03-03, while its own month_start = 2025-03-01, quarter = 1. This one row connects fact_sellout (whose week starts March 3rd) and fact_sellin (whose month starts March 1st) — both see the same calendar, just through different columns of it.
lessons.reads: One "quarter = 1" slicer filters weekly sales and monthly shipments at the same time — because both fact tables ultimately connect to the same date table.
lessons.wrong: Skip dim_date: build a slicer straight on week_start in fact_sellout, and expect it to affect fact_sellin the same way.
lessons.wrongWhy: fact_sellin has no row with date 2025-03-03 at all — the whole of March sits in one row dated 2025-03-01 there. A slicer built on one fact table's column finds no matches in the other: they literally hold different values in different columns, and no direct relationship between the two fact tables resolves that difference.
lessons.selfCheck: How many fact tables does your model have, and how many different time granularities among them (week, month)? More than one, and you need a shared calendar — otherwise one slicer will never tie them all together.

lessons.title: One date, two roles
lessons.why: A fact table has two dates: ordered and shipped. The requester asks for "revenue for March" — without saying which one. The answers differ, both are correct, and the choice between them falls to you — and then you need to be able to explain it.
lessons.form:
Both dates connect to the same calendar, not to two copies of it. One relationship stays active — the one most measures compute by.

The second relationship exists but is marked inactive. Whichever measure needs it specifically switches it on explicitly, via USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE.
lessons.example: In fact_sellin, shipping lags ordering by 2 to 11 days, and 1,979 of 15,362 orders ship the following month. March 2025: by order date ¥3,303,414, by ship date ¥3,570,458. The active relationship is on order_date; a "Revenue by shipment" measure switches context to ship_date.
lessons.reads: A ¥267,000 gap for one month isn't a mistake in either number — it's two answers to two different questions: "how much was ordered in March" and "how much shipped in March."
lessons.wrong: Add a second date table to the model — a separate calendar for the ship date — and connect each to its own column.
lessons.wrongWhy: It formally works, but the field list ends up with two "Year" fields, two "Quarter" fields, and two slicers for people to guess between. Worse: one slicer stops filtering both measures at once — pick a year on the first calendar, and you won't narrow the measure computing off the second, leaving numbers for different periods sitting side by side on the report.
lessons.selfCheck: How many dates does your fact table have, and how many calendars does your model have? If there's more than one calendar, ask yourself what slicer someone will put on the page — and what happens to the second measure.

lessons.title: Many-to-many and the bridge table
lessons.why: Sometimes there genuinely isn't a way to connect two tables directly: the key repeats on both sides, and that isn't a data defect, it's the nature of the relationship. Joining it directly gets you exactly the kind of inflated sums that are impossible to explain.
lessons.form:
The tell for many-to-many is mechanical: the relationship's key isn't unique in either table.

The fix is a bridge table: a separate table of unique pairs, which both sides connect to as one-to-many. No direct relationship gets created between the original tables at all.
lessons.example: dim_product (47 rows, 9 brands) and dim_promo (89 promos, the same 9 brands). Brand repeats on both sides. The "product × promo" bridge holds 465 unique pairs: for brand «Nettora» that's 5 products × 10 promos = 50 bridge rows.
lessons.reads: Every bridge row is one specific "this product took part in this promo" pair. Both source tables connect to the bridge the way a lookup connects to a fact table, and the key no longer repeats on either relationship.
lessons.wrong: Link dim_product and dim_promo directly on the brand column, since it exists in both tables.
lessons.wrongWhy: A relationship like that matches group to group, not row to row, and every pair inside a group becomes its own row in the calculation. That's exactly how revenue in mdl-013 grew from ¥126,911,191 to ¥1,262,668,596 — exactly tenfold, matching the number of promos per brand. A model usually won't even let you make a relationship like this active, but a join made in a query that bypasses the model is protected by nothing.
lessons.selfCheck: Take the relationship's key and count row totals and distinct-value totals in both tables. Matches anywhere — an ordinary relationship. Matches nowhere — you need a bridge.

lessons.title: CALCULATE: replacing context
lessons.why: CALCULATE is DAX's central function and the biggest source of confusion. It gets read like SQL's WHERE, and up to a point that works. It breaks on the very first report that already has a slicer on the page: WHERE would add a condition, CALCULATE will replace it.
lessons.form:
CALCULATE(expression, condition) evaluates the expression not in the current filter context, but in a modified one.

A condition on a column REPLACES every filter already on that column — and leaves filters on other columns untouched.
lessons.example: Measure "Aqualis Revenue" = CALCULATE(SUM(revenue), brand = «Aqualis»). The page has a region slicer for «Tokyo». Result: ¥1,323,959 — the region filter survives, because region and brand are different columns; a brand slicer, if there were one, would get overwritten.
lessons.reads: The condition inside CALCULATE swapped out the brand filter and left the region filter untouched. Tokyo's full revenue, for comparison, is ¥8,876,489.
lessons.wrong: Assume CALCULATE(SUM(revenue), brand = «Aqualis»), with brand «Nettora» selected in a slicer, gives an intersection — meaning zero, since a product can't be two brands at once.
lessons.wrongWhy: There's no intersection: the condition inside CALCULATE doesn't add to the slicer, it replaces it. The measure returns «Aqualis»'s full revenue, as if there were no brand slicer at all. This is the most common cause of "why is my measure ignoring my filter" — it isn't ignoring it, it's overwriting it.
lessons.selfCheck: Before writing a condition inside CALCULATE, ask: could there already be a slicer on this column? If yes, you'll overwrite it. Need to preserve it and add your own on top — use KEEPFILTERS.

lessons.title: Context transition
lessons.why: The same formula, written as a column and invoked as a measure, gives different numbers. This isn't a bug or a syntax quirk — it's the one place in DAX where one kind of context silently turns into another, and without understanding it, reading someone else's measures is impossible.
lessons.form:
Context transition happens inside CALCULATE (and inside any measure, because invoking a measure is implicitly wrapped in CALCULATE).

The current row stops being just a row and turns into a filter: "every row where the key columns' values match this one's."
lessons.example: dim_product has 9 brands and 47 products. The measure [Total Revenue] = SUM(revenue) gives ¥126,911,191 across the whole database. Invoked in the «Fruvia» brand row of a matrix, the same measure gives ¥25,465,980 — row context turned into a filter, "brand = «Fruvia»."
lessons.reads: A measure doesn't know about a "current row" — it only knows about filters. Context transition is the mechanism that turns one into the other.
lessons.wrong: Expect a calculated column "=SUM(fact_sellout[revenue])" in dim_product to show its own product's revenue — by analogy with how the same measure behaves in a matrix.
lessons.wrongWhy: An ordinary calculated column has no context transition: SUM sees an empty filter context and aggregates the whole table, giving ¥126,911,191 in every row of the lookup. To get its own product's revenue, the formula needs wrapping in CALCULATE — that's exactly what translates row context into a filter.
lessons.selfCheck: When you see a measure inside an iterator or a calculated column, ask: is there a CALCULATE here — explicit, or implicit via invoking a measure? If so, the current row has already become a filter, and the result needs reading with that in mind.

lessons.title: Time intelligence
lessons.why: YTD, last year, a rolling average — half of what anyone ever asks a BI analyst for. The functions for this look like ready-made buttons, but every one of them does the same thing to the date filter: replaces it with a different set of dates.
lessons.form:
Every time intelligence function is a wrapper around CALCULATE with a swapped-out calendar filter.

TOTALYTD replaces the current period with "from the start of the year through the current date." SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR replaces it with the same period a year earlier. DATESINPERIOD replaces it with an arbitrary interval.
lessons.example: March 2025 revenue is ¥4,694,330. SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR swaps the filter to March 2024 and returns ¥4,392,846; that gives 6.9% growth. TOTALYTD on the same cell swaps the filter to January-March 2025 and gives ¥12,566,159.
lessons.reads: None of these functions stores separate data — all three compute the same SUM(revenue), just under different sets of dates substituted in for the current one.
lessons.wrong: Apply these functions to a calendar that has gaps — a date table built from dates that actually occurred in the facts, say.
lessons.wrongWhy: Time intelligence functions assume a continuous calendar: they compute "the prior period" by shifting dates, not by looking up a neighbouring row. A gap in the calendar silently breaks that shift. In our model, dim_date holds 912 consecutive days with not a single gap — 2025 is represented by all 365 of its days, including ones with no sales at all.
lessons.selfCheck: Check the calendar for continuity: its row count should equal the difference between its earliest and latest dates, plus one. If it doesn't match, complete the calendar first, then write YTD.

lessons.title: Power Query and the preparation layer
lessons.why: Dirt in the data always has to be cleaned; the only question is where. The temptation is to clean it in a measure, because that is closest at hand and needs no refresh. The price of that decision becomes clear six months later, when there are forty measures and each has its own version of the cleanup.
lessons.form:
Three places you can clean, in order of preference:

  at the source — if you have any influence there: the fix reaches every consumer at once
  in Power Query — at load time, once per model, before the data lands in tables
  in a measure — only what depends on the evaluation context and cannot be computed in advance
lessons.example: In staging_raw_sellout one outlet, «Ichiba #1026», appears in four spellings: Ichiba and Itiba, with and without spaces at the edges. Plus 110 duplicates, 84 empty units and four different date formats across 3,110 rows. All of it is fixed in Power Query, once, at load time.
lessons.reads: After the preparation layer, one outlet enters the model instead of four, and no measure ever knows this problem existed.
lessons.wrong: Leave it as is and write TRIM with an Itiba-to-Ichiba replacement into every measure: CALCULATE(SUM(revenue), SUBSTITUTE(TRIM(customer_name), "Itiba", "Ichiba") = ...).
lessons.wrongWhy: First, this repeats in every measure the outlet name appears in, and one day those copies will disagree. Second, the outlet slicer will still show four variants of one «Ichiba» — a measure cleans its own calculation, not what the person sees in the filter list. Third, a formula like that is evaluated on every query, whereas Power Query would have done the work once overnight.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask of every cleanup: does its result depend on what is selected in the report? If not, it belongs in Power Query or at the source, not in a measure.

lessons.title: Slowly changing dimensions
lessons.why: A customer moved to another region, a product was reassigned to another category, a rep was moved to another team. An ordinary lookup table holds only the current value — and the entire sales history is instantly rewritten retroactively, without a trace in the report.
lessons.form:
SCD type 1 — overwrite: only the current value is kept, history is lost.

SCD type 2 — versioning: every change adds a new row with its own validity range (valid from / valid to), and the fact references the version that was current at the time of the event.
lessons.example: dim_customer holds 144 retail outlets and 16 regions, and every outlet has one region — the current one. If an outlet moved from «Tokyo» to «Kanagawa», a "sales by region for 2024" report will show its entire history in the new region, as if it had always been there.
lessons.reads: There is no error in the data: the lookup table honestly answers "where is this outlet now". The report was simply asking a different question — "where was it at the time of the sale".
lessons.wrong: Solve the problem by adding a "previous region" column to the lookup table.
lessons.wrongWhy: That covers exactly one move. The second move needs a "region before last", and so on — and more importantly, none of those columns answers which region was in effect on a specific sale date. SCD2 solves the problem generally: a customer gets as many rows as they have had states, and the fact references the right one by date.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask of every lookup attribute: if it changes, should old reports change along with it, or stay as they were? The latter means you need SCD2.

lessons.title: Incremental refresh
lessons.why: The model refreshes overnight and rereads the entire history. While the data is small, nobody notices. Once the refresh window stops fitting into the night, it turns out 90% of the work is being done for data that has not changed in years.
lessons.form:
The fact table is sliced into partitions by date. Only the partitions changes could have arrived in get refreshed — usually the last few weeks or months.

The rest stay as they are and are not reread at all.
lessons.example: fact_sellout holds 118,449 rows over two and a half years: 48,391 for 2024, 47,122 for 2025 and 22,936 for 2026. The last three months account for 11,353 rows, less than a tenth. Refreshing only those means doing a tenth of the work instead of all of it.
lessons.reads: 2024's data will never change again, yet it is reread every night on equal terms with the fresh rows. Partitioning by date removes exactly that work.
lessons.wrong: Configure incremental refresh and carry on editing historical data — correcting errors in last year's sales retroactively, say.
lessons.wrongWhy: A partition that is no longer refreshed lives a life of its own: a correction in the source simply never reaches it, and the model will spend years showing the old version of the figure without giving any sign of the discrepancy. Incremental refresh is a contract stating that history is immutable, and it has to be either honoured or broken deliberately by reloading the partition by hand.
lessons.selfCheck: Before switching incremental refresh on, ask the business: is anything corrected retroactively, and how far back? The depth of corrections is what sets the boundary the partitions must refresh to.

lessons.title: Model size and speed
lessons.why: The model has bloated, the report takes half a minute to open — and the first instinct is usually to start deleting rows. That is almost always beside the point: the engine stores data by column and compresses it by the number of distinct values, not by the number of rows.
lessons.form:
A column's cost is determined by its cardinality — the number of distinct values.

A column with 47 values across 118,449 rows compresses to almost nothing. A column with 118,449 distinct values does not compress at all and becomes the most expensive one in the model.
lessons.example: fact_sellout has 118,449 rows. product_id has 47 distinct values, week_start 131, units 154, revenue 86,389. And sellout_id, the row surrogate key, is distinct across all 118,449 — the most expensive column in the table, and one nobody will ever ask for in a report.
lessons.reads: Removing sellout_id alone from the model strips more weight than deleting half the rows — and costs you not a single reporting capability.
lessons.wrong: Shrink the model by trimming history: drop 2024 so the row count halves.
lessons.wrongWhy: The rows halve, but the distinct values in the expensive columns barely do: prices, amounts and identifiers repeat little between years. The gain will be far smaller than expected, and year-over-year comparison is lost for good. Start with columns the report does not need at all, and only then discuss the depth of history.
lessons.selfCheck: Sort the table's columns by distinct-value count and look at the top ones. Ask of each: does anyone display it in a report or filter by it? If not, it does not belong in the model.
